title: Research
text: My research examines how incentives and connections between people, firms and countries shape economic outcomes.

title: Research
text:
Working Papers
Incentive Design on Networks (with A. Daripa and S. Kapur)
How can we design incentives to encourage the formation of productive connections when individual incentives do not necessarily lead to socially optimal outcomes?
We design a mechanism for network formation with privately known productivities that implements the socially optimal network through transfers based on opportunity costs, ensuring ex post incentive compatibility, pairwise stability, and budget balance.
Read working paper on SSRN

Network Structures and Credit Rating (with A. Daripa and S. Kapur)
How can we design a mechanism to infer private information about agents’ types by observing the connections they form?
We study whether productivity-consistent credit ratings can be inferred from endogenous network structure, showing that under suitable link costs equilibrium networks separate types and sustain ratings aligned with productivity.
Read working paper on SSRN

title: Research
text:
Published Papers
Too Much Finance: Mechanisms That Harm Growth and Policy Implications (with A. Daripa and S. Kapur), The Manchester School, 2026, 1–20.
When can the expansion of finance harm economic growth, and what does this imply for policy?
Journal article

Decentralized Defence of a (Directed) Network Structure, Defence and Peace Economics, 2020.
When do individual decisions about security protect a network as well as coordinated decisions?
I analyse how agents in a directed network allocate defence resources under external threats, showing that decentralised choices can be efficient with a strategic attacker but generally diverge from the social optimum under random attacks.
Journal article

Centrality in Trade Networks and Investment in Security (with V. Bove and L. Elia), Peace Economics, Peace Science and Public Policy, 2016.
How does a country’s position in global trade networks relate to its military spending?
We show that a country’s position in global trade networks—measured by network centrality—systematically shapes and constrains its military spending decisions.
Journal article

title: Marco Pelliccia
text:
About
I am an economist and Managing Consultant at SQW. My background combines research in network economics and game theory with quantitative modelling and applied data analysis. I am interested in how incentives and connections between people, organisations, and markets shape economic outcomes.
Alongside my role at SQW, I continue to teach part time at Heriot-Watt University until December 2026.

title: Marco Pelliccia
text:
Background
I hold a PhD in Economics from Birkbeck, University of London, where I specialised in network economics and game theory. I have over ten years’ experience in higher education, including research and teaching in microeconomics, game theory, and economic policy.
I have also completed the MIT Applied Data Science Program, developing applied skills in machine learning and statistical modelling. My research and independent projects bring these interests together.

title: Projects
text: These independent projects apply economic reasoning, data analysis and simulation to decision problems. They illustrate my methods and interests alongside my academic research.

title: Projects
section: Loan Default Prediction and Lending Decision Analysis
text:
Loan Default Prediction and Lending Decision Analysis
Question. How should a lender assess default predictions when false approvals and false rejections have different costs?
Approach. Using the HMEQ home-equity loan dataset, I compare logistic regression, tree-based models, ensemble methods and XGBoost. The analysis considers classification performance, decision thresholds and the expected loss from lending errors.
Insight and relevance. Model assessment needs to reflect the costs of the decisions it informs. The project connects predictive modelling with lending decisions through expected-loss analysis.
Limitations. Conclusions depend on this dataset and the assumed costs of lending errors. Performance in a live lending setting would require separate validation.
Tools and methods: Python, scikit-learn, XGBoost, threshold optimisation, expected-loss analysis and SHAP.
View project on GitHub

title: Projects
text:
Network Segregation Model
Question. How can individual choices about whom to connect to produce segregation across a network?
Approach. This NetLogo simulation adapts Schelling’s segregation model to network formation. Agents weigh the cost of links against a preference for having at least a chosen share of neighbours from their own group.
Insight and relevance. Individual link choices can produce segregated networks even when agents gain no additional benefit from similarity beyond their chosen threshold. The model provides a way to explore how individual incentives and network effects interact.
Limitations. This is an illustrative model. Outcomes depend on the behavioural rules, initial network and parameter choices.
Tools and methods: NetLogo, agent-based simulation and network analysis.


Model details and instructions

Agents belong to one of two groups and evaluate the share of same-type neighbours in their immediate network. The model uses a threshold-flat utility function: agents want at least a chosen share of similar neighbours, but receive no further benefit from homogeneity once that threshold is reached.
Links are costly to maintain. Unhappy agents may cut, create or rewire links when doing so improves their utility.
To run the model, choose the number of agents with the buttons slider, set %-similar-wanted, and adjust the link cost and payoff parameters. Press Setup to create an initial random network, then Go to let agents update their links.
Outputs include the percentage of happy agents, the number of links, the share of same-type links, the clustering coefficient and average welfare.
